e.t: Abadōn, also rendered Avathon, is a proper name rather than a common descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in 1 Chronicles, as the name of individuals in genealogical lists. The supplied lexical meaning identifies the name itself but does not provide a broader definition or explanation of its significance. Its precise role in any one occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Abōr, also rendered Avor, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Kings: 17:6 and 18:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise geographic or narrative significance cannot be stated more specifically. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name Abor or Avor.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person or named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is represented by the names “Adasai” and “Athase.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 24:6. Since it is a name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it distinguishes the individual named in that passage rather than describing that individual’s character or role. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific place in the passage.

This adjective describes someone or something connected with murdering a brother. It presents the act in a direct, severe way, identifying the killing of one’s own brother rather than violence in general. As an adjective, it describes a person or action instead of naming the act by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 10:3. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wording, but its basic meaning remains focused on the murder of a brother.

Aingadin, also rendered Engathin, is a proper name for a place rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 47:10. The available meaning identifies the name itself but does not provide a further definition or explain the place’s significance. Its precise role in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and context.

Alexandreia is a proper name for Alexandria, identifying a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The alternate rendering “Aleksanthria” reflects the same name, not a different idea. In the Greek of the Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:1. Because the verse text is not included here, the name itself is the clear meaning available.

This verb means “indicate” or “appoint”: it can point something out or designate someone for a role. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, it occurs 12 times. Its basic idea may involve making something known or setting someone or something in a designated place or position. The surrounding wording determines which aspect is prominent in a particular verse; the word itself expresses clear indication or assignment.

This adverb means “back again,” describing a return to an earlier place, condition, or action. It points to something happening once more or being restored to a previous position. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:21. The surrounding verse is needed to know exactly what is returning or happening again there, but the word itself carries the simple idea of going or coming back again.

gl: one taken in war and sold as a slave; captive
d: one taken in war and sold as a slave; captive

e.h: A Captive Sold as a Slave
e.t: This noun means “one taken in war and sold as a slave; captive.” It refers to a person seized during conflict and treated as property for sale. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 7:5. Its central idea is not simply that someone was defeated, but that the defeated person was forcibly taken and reduced to slavery. The surrounding verse gives the specific setting in which this word appears.

This noun means “heap of live coals”: a pile of glowing, burning embers gathered together. It refers to the coals themselves rather than to a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach 11:32 and 4 Maccabees 9:20. Since no verse text is provided, the surrounding context would determine whether the image is being used literally or as part of a comparison. Its central meaning remains a concentrated heap of burning coals.

This Greek LXX verb means “sound”: it describes something producing or giving off a sound. As a verb, it points to the action of sounding rather than to a sound as an object or name. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 18:10. The surrounding verse is needed to determine what is sounding there, but the word itself expresses the act of sounding.

This Greek LXX verb means to “weep aloud,” describing crying expressed openly rather than silent sorrow. It is a verb, so it portrays the act of vocal, audible weeping. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Proverbs and Jeremiah. Its basic meaning remains focused on the outward expression of grief through loud crying; the surrounding passage determines whose grief is being described and why.

This Greek LXX verb means “arrange to leave” or “say goodbye.” It describes taking leave, especially when someone departs from a place or from other people. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “breathe hard; gasp for breath.” It describes the physical act of breathing with difficulty, especially when a person is short of breath or laboring to draw breath. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 31:19. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation there; the word itself centers on labored breathing.

This LXX Greek verb means “dawn.” It describes the beginning or arrival of daylight—the point when light starts to appear. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, with all seven occurrences in Leviticus. Thus, it is an action word for daybreak, while the surrounding passage determines how that idea functions in each sentence. It is not a noun naming dawn, but a verb describing dawn’s appearing.

This word means “starting-point” or “base”: the place, condition, or resource from which something begins or proceeds. As a noun, it can describe a foundation or an available point of departure rather than the action that follows. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, appearing in Proverbs, Ezekiel, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is beginning or being supported in the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “pace”—the measured rate or movement of someone or something. It can refer to how quickly a person proceeds, or to a step or progression considered in relation to distance or time. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, including several occurrences in 2 Kings. Its basic idea remains focused on measured movement rather than speed in the abstract. The precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Bakchides is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also rendered Vakkhithis. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 21 times, appearing chiefly in 1 Maccabees and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact significance comes from the person identified by this name in each passage, while the word itself functions simply as a personal designation.

Berchia, also rendered Verkhia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 12:3. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand the person’s role in that specific setting.

This noun refers to a council chamber or senate-house—the place where a council or senate gathers to deliberate. It names a meeting place, rather than the council members themselves. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in deuterocanonical books: three times in 1 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains focused on the physical setting where formal public discussion or decision-making takes place.

This Greek LXX word means “noise,” referring to a sound or tumult that can be heard. It can function as a noun for the sound itself or describe something associated with such noise. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Job, Joel, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an audible disturbance or rushing sound.

This adjective describes something as “suitable to one’s birth.” It relates a person or thing to what is fitting for the birth or family status being considered. As an adjective, it characterizes a noun rather than naming an action or object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:2; the surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely what it describes there.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut out the tongue,” describing the act of removing a person’s tongue. It is a precise action word rather than a general term for injury or speech. The verb appears three times in the deuterocanonical Greek writings: once in 2 Maccabees and twice in 4 Maccabees. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact force in each passage must be understood from its immediate context, but its basic meaning remains the same: to cut out the tongue.

This verb means “dismember”: to tear or divide a body into separate parts. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 3:96, so its normal meaning is clear even though the verse text is not included here. The surrounding passage would determine the precise force of the action in that occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “warp,” the lengthwise threads used in woven material. It names a part of the weaving structure rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Judges 16:13–14. The word’s precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the warp—the arranged threads through which other threads are woven.

This verb means “drive a chariot.” It describes the action of guiding or operating a chariot, focusing on the person handling the vehicle rather than on the chariot itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:30. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but the basic action remains clear: someone is driving a chariot.

This verb means “empower”: to give someone strength or ability to act. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes strengthening rather than merely possessing power. The word occurs three times, in two Psalms and Ecclesiastes, so its central idea is consistent while the surrounding passage determines who receives strength and for what purpose. Its meaning points to power being supplied or increased, enabling a person or action to become more capable.

This adjective means “ventriloquizing,” describing speech presented as though it comes from another voice or source. It is used in the Greek Old Testament, where it occurs 15 times across 14 verses. Its repeated appearance in passages about mediums and those claiming to communicate with the dead helps identify the kind of speech it describes, without making the word itself a title for a person. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Collect money” is the basic meaning of this Greek Old Testament verb. As a verb, it describes an action involving money rather than a person, place, or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Kings 12:5 and 2 Chronicles 34:14. Those references identify where it appears, but the precise force of each occurrence belongs to its surrounding verse and passage. In ordinary reading, the word points to the act of collecting money.

This verb means “greatly terrified”: it describes being overwhelmed by intense fear, not merely feeling uneasy. As a verb, it expresses the experience of becoming or being deeply frightened, rather than a mild concern or passing alarm. In the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “cast forth”: to throw or drive something out from a place or position. It describes a forceful sending away rather than simply moving something. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Judges, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom is being cast forth and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something beaten or made by beating it into shape. It refers to an object formed through worked material rather than something left in its natural state. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in descriptions connected with the shields and vessels of Solomon’s kingdom. Its core meaning remains “beaten; of beaten work,” while the surrounding noun identifies what has been fashioned in this way.

Elieli is a proper name—the personal name of an individual, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 8:20. The available lexical form gives the name as “Eliēli; Elili,” so it is best understood as a name to identify a person, not as a term to expand into a broader definition. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding genealogy and the person being named.

This Greek LXX verb expresses that something is acceptable or can be accepted. It describes acceptability rather than naming a person, object, or abstract quality. The word appears two times in the Greek Old Testament and related Deuterocanonical writings represented here, once in Daniel and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

gl: lie in wait for; lie in ambush
d: lie in wait for; lie in ambush

e.t: This verb means to lie in wait for someone or to lie in ambush, describing concealed waiting with the purpose of catching or attacking a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Judges, Job, and Lamentations. Its basic idea is purposeful, hidden waiting rather than ordinary patience or delay. The exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “intercede”: to appeal on behalf of another person. It describes someone stepping forward before another party with a request or plea for someone else. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 13 times, showing a repeated action rather than a single specialized use. Its precise force in any passage depends on who is interceding, whom they approach, and whose need or cause they present.

This verb means “outfox”: to outsmart or deceive someone by clever maneuvering. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it expresses the attempt to gain an advantage through trickery. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 8:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the idea of cleverly outwitting another person.

This adjective describes something that brings gain or benefit, making it profitable or advantageous. It can identify what is useful because it produces a favorable result or serves one's interests. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in the deuterocanonical book of Wisdom, at Wisdom 15:12. Without the verse text, its precise force there cannot be described further, but its basic sense is something beneficial or gainful.

This verb means to put a seal on something or to confirm it. It describes an act that marks, secures, or formally verifies something as established. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Nehemiah and once in Bel and the Dragon, showing this concrete sense in each occurrence. The word may refer either to the physical act of sealing or, by extension, to giving confirmation. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX adjective means “seven thousand,” describing a quantity of seven groups of one thousand. It functions as a number word, identifying how many people or items are being counted rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, including passages in Numbers, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Job. Its exact referent—whether people, animals, or possessions—comes from the surrounding sentence, but the numerical meaning remains seven thousand.

This word means “of the desert.” It is a noun describing something associated with, belonging to, or connected with a desert. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 11:12. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense points to the desert as the relevant place or setting. It is not a broad term for every kind of wilderness or remote region; the supplied meaning specifically identifies the desert.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “find” or “discover.” It describes coming upon something, locating it, or recognizing what has been uncovered. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Samuel, Chronicles, Daniel, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused on reaching or gaining knowledge of what was previously missing, hidden, or unknown. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on locating something physically or discovering it through understanding.

This noun describes good courage—a strong, confident spirit that enables someone to face difficulty with resolve. It can refer to inner bravery or an uplifted, courageous attitude rather than mere excitement or confidence without cause. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains courage that gives a person strength to stand firm when circumstances are demanding.

Zamma is a proper name, used to identify a named individual rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. Its lexical gloss is simply “Zamma,” so no broader meaning is established here. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:27. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding genealogy and verse text, which are not included here.

Enremmon is a proper name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It is represented as “Ēnremmōn; Inremmon” in the Greek Old Testament. The name appears only once in this corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:32. Because it is a single personal or place-name occurrence without surrounding verse text here, its specific referent cannot be identified further from the name alone.

This Greek LXX noun means “minister”: a person identified by service or attendance in a role of ministry. It designates someone who serves, rather than an object, place, or action. The word occurs 56 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense appears across many passages. The precise responsibility of the minister depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

The word is a proper name meaning “Thrax” or “Thraks.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 12:35. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse context is needed to determine exactly whom or what the name designates there.

This word is a proper name, referring to Iezabēl, also given as “Iezavil.” It is a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times across 20 verses, from 1 Kings through 2 Kings. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

gl: piece of timber used instead of a bond-stone
d: piece of timber used instead of a bond-stone

e.t: This word means a piece of timber used instead of a bond-stone. It names a physical building material: a wooden piece serving as a substitute for a stone that would normally tie or strengthen part of a structure. It is a noun, so it identifies the object itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek text of Sirach, it appears once, at Sirach 22:16. Its exact significance there depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “horse captain,” referring to a person who leads or oversees horses in a military setting. It functions as a title for an officer connected with mounted forces, rather than describing an animal or an ordinary rider. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears once, in 2 Samuel 1:6. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense identifies a captain associated with horses.

Ismael, also rendered Izmel, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears 44 times across 41 verses, beginning in Genesis 16:11 and occurring later in Genesis, Chronicles, Kings, Jeremiah, and other books. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is the identification of the individual called Ismael; the surrounding passage is needed to understand what is being said about him in any particular verse.

Kabasaēl, also rendered Kavasel, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:22. The name identifies a particular person or place in that passage, but the available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain which one or add further significance. Its meaning is therefore best presented as the name Kabasaēl or Kavasel, with its precise reference determined by the passage.

This adjective means “made of reed,” describing something formed from or consisting of reed material. It is a specific material word rather than a general description of plants or grasses. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in 2 Kings 18:21, Isaiah 36:6, and Ezekiel 29:6. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: something reed-made or reed-like in material.

Kappadokia is a proper name for a place, also rendered Kappathokia. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in Amos. Because it is a place-name rather than a common noun, its meaning is primarily identifying a geographic region named in those passages. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide surrounding verse text or further description of the region.

This noun means “speck,” referring to a very small particle or fragment. It describes something tiny rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Genesis 8:11. The word’s basic sense is therefore narrow and concrete: a small bit that can be noticed or observed. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object being described there.

This Greek LXX verb means “list”: to name or set out people or things one by one. It describes the act of making an enumeration rather than expressing a feeling, quality, or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here—once in Deuteronomy and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being listed and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the orderly naming or recording of items.

This noun means “pouring over,” describing the action or movement of liquid being poured across or upon something. It names an act rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 36:16. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the spreading or flowing of something poured over a surface or area.

This verb means “have mercy”: to respond with compassion toward someone in need or distress. It describes an action of showing pity rather than merely noticing another person’s suffering. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea remains an active, compassionate response toward another person.

Kēraos; Kiraos is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:44. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its broader identity or the person connected with it cannot be stated more precisely here. Its role is to identify an individual in that passage.

This verb means “seize” or “retain”: to take hold of something or continue holding it. It describes an active grasping or keeping rather than a passive condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 142 times, so its basic idea is used across many kinds of statements. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on taking hold, holding firmly, or keeping possession. Its lexical identity is κρατέω, rendered here as a verb.

This verb means “employed by,” expressing the act or condition of being engaged in someone’s service. It describes a person whose work or service is directed toward another party. The word appears 89 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, beginning in Exodus and continuing through 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Maiani” or “Meani.” It identifies a named individual, place, or group in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available information does not specify which kind of name it is. It occurs only once in this corpus, at Joshua 15:34. Its precise referent must therefore be identified from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name itself.

Membra, also rendered Memvra, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named person or place, but the available word-level information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 15:35. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the verse text is not included here.

Mii, also written Mi, is a proper name—a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:46. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so its precise role in that passage cannot be explained here. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal name “Mii” or “Mi.”

This word describes something aromatic or perfumed—something carrying a pleasant fragrance. It can function as an adjective for a scented substance or as a noun referring to such a perfumed preparation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Exodus and Song of Songs. Its uses include fragrant preparations and perfume-related language, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording. The basic idea remains a pleasing, intentionally prepared scent rather than an ordinary or accidental smell.

Nargalasar is a proper name, referring to someone or something identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. The word itself does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it functions as a specific name. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Jeremiah 46:3. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise reference there cannot be explained further from the word alone.

This Greek LXX noun means “girl,” referring to a female child or young female. It is a straightforward personal description rather than a title, action, or abstract quality. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Old Testament writings represented in this corpus, showing that it is used across several books. Its precise age range or significance in a particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding words and situation.

This LXX adverb means “right now,” pointing to the present moment or to something happening immediately. It draws attention to what is true, occurring, or being asked at the current time, rather than to a distant past or future. The word appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so its basic force remains consistent across different passages. The surrounding verse determines exactly what present situation it highlights.

This word is the proper name “Noman,” identifying a named person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:41, and is rendered “Noman.” Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s precise referent in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a specific name: Noman.

Oziēl is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears in the Greek Septuagint as “Oziēl” or “Ozil.” The name occurs 21 times in the Old Testament portion of the Septuagint, across genealogical and historical passages. Because the supplied meaning is a name identification rather than a definition, its significance depends on which person bearing the name is being mentioned in a particular passage.

This adjective describes writing done swiftly—“swift-writing” or “writing fast.” It portrays the manner of writing rather than naming the writer or the subject being written about. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 44:2. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force there, but its basic meaning remains focused on speed and readiness in writing.

This noun refers to the means by which someone exists or to possessions held as property. It can therefore point either to a person’s subsistence—the resources needed to live—or to property considered as what belongs to someone. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:28. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which sense is intended there.

This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “five times”. It indicates that something happens or is done on five occasions. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 13:19, so its broader use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its meaning remains straightforward: it describes the number of times an action occurs, rather than naming a person, object, or place.

This Greek LXX verb means “tear off”: to pull something away by force or separation. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented in this corpus, once in Genesis and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being torn away and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains forceful removal or separation.

This verb means “steer”: to direct or guide something in a chosen direction. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:1. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of steering or directing. This adjective means “gray” or “grizzled,” describing a grayish or grizzled appearance. It is a descriptive word rather than a name or action, and its ordinary sense concerns visible color or age-related appearance. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Leviticus 19:32. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a description of something gray or grizzled.

This adjective means “purple,” describing something having the color purple. It is a straightforward color word rather than a title, action, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Numbers, Esther, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. The surrounding verse determines what purple object or clothing is being described in each passage, but the word itself identifies the color. Its precise reference changes with the noun it describes, while its basic meaning remains consistent.

This verb means to torture someone beforehand—to subject a person to painful testing or torment before a later event or action. It describes an act rather than a person, object, or general condition. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. The wording can therefore point to prior torture or torment, while the surrounding sentence determines who is being tortured and what follows. Its basic sense remains focused on inflicting suffering in advance.

This adverb means acting eagerly, willingly, or with a ready inclination. It describes the manner in which someone does something, emphasizing inner readiness rather than reluctance or compulsion. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in 2 Chronicles, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The precise force in any particular sentence depends on what action it modifies, but its central idea is a willing and eager response.

This noun means a shoot or twig—a young, slender growth from a plant or tree. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Job, where it names a small but living part of vegetation. The basic idea is something that grows from a larger plant and may suggest renewed growth or fragile life, though its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is distinct from a general word for a whole tree or plant.

Samoue, also rendered Samue, is a proper name referring to a person identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 12:18. The available wording establishes the name itself but does not provide a further ordinary meaning or description. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s role there.

Selei, also rendered Seli, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 1 Kings: once at 1 Kings 16:28 and again at 1 Kings 22:42. The available information identifies the name itself, but does not provide a separate lexical meaning beyond the personal-name forms Selei and Seli.

This word is a proper name, given as “Sēlōn; Silon.” It functions as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general.
